analysis.one_liner: Allows Americans to buy lower-cost prescription drugs from certified Canadian pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2017 with no cosponsors and died in the Senate health committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Health and Human Services to write rules, within 180 days, letting individuals import a 90-day personal supply of a prescription drug from a Canadian pharmacy certified by HHS. The drug would have to be identical in active ingredient, dose, and form to the FDA-approved version, filled with a valid US prescription, and dispensed by a Canadian-licensed pharmacist. Controlled substances, biologics, and several other sensitive drug types would be excluded, and HHS would publish a list of approved pharmacies.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay US prices for prescription drugs, especially people who take expensive maintenance medications like insulin, blood thinners, or heart drugs and pay out of pocket. Canadian licensed pharmacies would gain a new customer base.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans paying high US drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require HHS to issue regulations within 180 days permitting individuals to import prescription drugs from approved Canadian pharmacies, capped at a 90-day personal supply and filled with a valid US prescription.

Only pharmacies certified by HHS — licensed in Canada, at least five years old, with quality-assurance and grievance processes — could sell to Americans, and HHS would publish an approved list on the FDA website, giving consumers a vetted channel rather than a gray market.
Imported drugs would have to have the same active ingredients, dosage form, and strength as the FDA-approved version, so consumers would be buying the same medicine at Canadian prices.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies, which currently sell the same drugs at higher prices in the US than in Canada, would lose some US sales to cheaper imports. US pharmacies and the FDA would also bear costs — lost revenue for pharmacies and a new certification and oversight workload for regulators.

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes controlled substances, biologics, infused and intravenous drugs, refrigerated products, and biotechnology-derived drugs, which would leave out many of the newest and most expensive medicines — including insulin analogues and monoclonal antibody drugs — limiting how much consumers could actually save.

Critics of drug importation have long argued the FDA cannot fully verify the safety of medicines sold abroad, raising the risk of counterfeit or mishandled products reaching consumers; the bill addresses this with a certification program and mandatory lab testing, but it cannot eliminate the risk entirely.
It would add a regulatory burden on HHS and the FDA to certify pharmacies, run quality-assurance testing through approved laboratories, and police compliance, an ongoing federal oversight cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is real but narrower than the title suggests: it would create a safe, legal way to buy many common brand-name and generic drugs at Canadian prices, but the exclusions keep the priciest biologic drugs out of reach. The costs fall mainly on drug manufacturers, who price the US market higher than every other developed country, and on regulators, who would take on a certification workload. On balance the savings to patients would outweigh the safety and administrative costs, which is why similar proposals keep reappearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the Safe and Affordable Drugs from Canada Act on January 9, 2017.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, and no further action was ever recorded.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill receiving a floor vote or a committee vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical companies and US pharmacies, which kept selling at American prices without Canadian competition, were better off because the bill never moved; the committee chairman, who never scheduled it for consideration, did not have to take a position.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: US Senator from Arizona and the bill's sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on January 9, 2017.

against.name: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled the bill for consideration after it was referred; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has consistently lobbied against prescription drug importation bills, arguing they threaten drug safety and undermine manufacturers' revenue.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held, and the bill's only sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors, so no party split can be measured; a Republican sponsor made drug importation from Canada a nominally bipartisan issue but drew no colleagues to sign on.

industries.note: US prices for the same drugs are far higher than Canadian prices; allowing personal importation would divert sales to cheaper Canadian pharmacies. Consumers' savings would come directly out of manufacturers' US revenue.
Certified Canadian pharmacies would gain a legal, government-listed channel to sell 90-day supplies to American patients. Their gain runs alongside consumers' savings.
American pharmacies would lose some prescription revenue to Canadian competitors charging less for the same drugs.
